headline.en: A stave is five lines. Every line and every space is one note, and higher on the stave is higher in pitch. Your do sits where your own note is.

detail.en: Each one is the next note up
Every line here starts on it
Medium volume; stop if anything tightens or hurts

text.en: Watch the stave while it plays, then sing it back: do, re, mi, re, do.
Your turn to read. Look first, then sing it as the notes light: the names are under them.

measures.en: Scored on each note's pitch.

headline.en: A step goes from a line to the next space, or a space to the next line. Up the stave is up in pitch.

detail.en: Line, space, line: three notes in a row

text.en: Read up to so, names under the notes.
Now back down. The names are faint: read the stave first.

measures.en: Scored on each note's pitch.

headline.en: Real tunes turn: up a little, back, then on. Follow the notes, not a pattern.

text.en: A line that turns, names faint.
Another, with no names at all.

measures.en: Scored on each note's pitch.

text.en: The treble clef is a fancy letter G. Its curl wraps around the line where G sits, which is why it's also called the G clef.

headline.en: A line you haven't heard, two bars long. Look, find do, then read it straight through.

text.en: Read it cold: no names.

measures.en: Scored on each note's pitch.

headline.en: Do, mi and so are the notes of your home chord. On the stave each sits two steps above the last: line to line, or space to space.

detail.en: Jumps over one line or space

text.en: Watch the skips while they play, then sing them back.
Read the skips, names under the notes.

measures.en: Scored on each note's pitch.

headline.en: Many tunes start below do, on the so beneath it, and leap up home. On the stave it's a skip and a step lower.

detail.en: So to do, like a call

text.en: So below do, then home: names faint.
Down to so, up through the chord, no names.

measures.en: Scored on each note's pitch.

headline.en: Now lines mix steps and skips. A step goes to the very next line or space; a skip jumps one.

text.en: Steps and skips, names faint.
And again, no names.

measures.en: Scored on each note's pitch.

text.en: The bass clef is a fancy letter F. Its two dots sit either side of the line where F sits, which is why it's also called the F clef.

headline.en: You know this tune by ear. Now read it: Ode to Joy's second line, four bars, from the stave alone.

detail.en: With one dotted note near the end

text.en: Ode to Joy's second line, no names.

measures.en: Scored on each note's pitch.

headline.en: Now the notes' shapes tell you how long. A filled note with a stem is one beat; a hollow one is two. A rest is a beat of silence that still counts.

detail.en: Filled, with a stem: one beat

text.en: Count in with the clicks, then read it: names faint.

measures.en: Scored on each note's pitch, and when it starts.

text.en: Again, no names. Hold each long note its full two beats.

measures.en: Scored on each note's pitch, and when it starts.

headline.en: A dot makes a note half as long again. A dotted minim is three beats, a whole bar of a waltz.

text.en: A waltz in threes: names faint.
A dotted crotchet, then a short note: long, short. No names.

measures.en: Scored on each note's pitch, and when it starts.

headline.en: A quaver is half a beat. It has a flag, or it's joined to its neighbour by a beam, and two fit in one beat.

text.en: Quick notes in pairs: names faint.

text.en: Quick and long together, with a rest that counts. No names.

text.en: A tempo mark like "M.M. = 72" stands for Maelzel's Metronome: Johann Maelzel patented the metronome in 1815, and composers began writing their speeds in its beats.

headline.en: Four bars with every kind of note so far, and rests. Look, count in, then read it in time.

detail.en: A slip? Catch the next beat

title.en: Sharps and flats at the start

text.en: Sharps in a key signature always come in the same order, F, C, G, D, A, E, B, and flats in the reverse order. Each new key a fifth higher adds the next sharp.

source.en: Wikipedia, "Key signature" (citing George Thaddeus Jones, Music Theory, 1974)

headline.en: Real music starts each line with a key signature: the sharps or flats there say which notes are always raised or lowered. Do moves with the key: it's the key's home note.

detail.en: The key of G: every F is F sharp
The key of F: every B is B flat

text.en: The flat, sharp and natural signs all grew from the letter b: the flat from a round b, the sharp and natural from a square one.

source.en: Wikipedia, "Accidental (music)", its history (citing Frederick Niecks, "The Flat, Sharp, and Natural: A Historical Sketch", 1889 to 1890)
